title: Slip stitch in depth
subtitle: Joining, travelling, seaming, and decorative surface work
excerpt: Slip stitch does more than close a round. This deep dive covers joining rounds cleanly, travelling across stitches without adding height, working a slip stitch seam, and using it for surface decoration on finished fabric.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Weldon's Practical Crochet, volumes 1 and 2 (Internet Archive). Slip stitch joining and surface crochet techniques.
heroPrompt: Close-up of a crochet slip stitch seam joining two finished squares, showing the neat ridge on the right side, cream and natural cotton yarn, plain pale background.

glossaryTerms.definition: The shortest crochet stitch: insert the hook, yarn over, pull through both the stitch and the loop on the hook in one motion. No height added.
Working slip stitches across the surface of a finished fabric to create raised lines, letters, or decorative motifs without adding fabric height.

content.text: The slip stitch works in one move: insert the hook, yarn over, pull through the stitch and the loop on the hook together. No height, no loops left mid-air. That single property makes it the connector stitch in every pattern that joins rounds, travels without adding fabric, or seams two finished pieces.

The foundations tutorial introduces the basic move. This one covers the four places a slip stitch actually matters: joining a round cleanly, travelling across a row, working a visible seam, and drawing
surface crochet
lines on top of finished fabric.
Joining a round without a twist
The single most common
slip stitch

error is a twisted join: the round closes but the beginning-of-round sits at an angle, so the fabric spirals slightly. The cause is almost always inserting the hook into the wrong loop of the turning chain.
Work the last stitch of the round. One loop remains on the hook.
Identify the turning chain that opened the round. In most patterns, a chain-3 stands in for the first treble. The top of that chain is the V-shaped pair of loops at the very tip.
Insert the hook from front to back under both loops of that V. Not into the side of the chain — under the top.
Yarn over, pull through both the chain and the loop on the hook. One loop on the hook. The round is joined.
Check the join from the right side: the stitch column at the join should sit vertically, not lean to one side.

attrs.title: One-size-up tip
attrs.body: Work joining slip stitches with a hook one size larger than the pattern hook. They pull tighter than every other stitch and the larger hook gives you the same tension as the body fabric.

content.text: Travelling across stitches

Patterns sometimes need the hook repositioned mid-row without breaking yarn. The instruction reads "sl st across N stitches" or "sl st to first ch-sp". Work one slip stitch into each stitch, going under both loops as normal. The slip stitches are invisible from the right side; they read as a flat line at the base of the next proper stitch.

Keep the tension very relaxed when travelling. A tight travel row pulls the edge in; a loose one loops out from the surface. Match the surrounding fabric tension as closely as you can, and use the one-size-up hook if the travel run is more than three or four stitches.
The slip stitch seam
A slip stitch seam joins two finished pieces with a decorative ridge on the right side. Use it on granny square blankets where the seam is a feature, not something to hide.
Hold two pieces with right sides together, matching edges stitch for stitch.
Insert the hook through both back loops of the top stitches on each piece, so you are going through four loops total.
Yarn over with the join yarn and draw through all four loops and the hook loop: one slip stitch worked through both pieces.
Continue stitch for stitch to the end. Fasten off and sew in the tail.
Open the seam to the right side. The unworked front loops of both pieces form a ridge along the join line.
Surface crochet

Surface crochet adds lines to the outside of a piece without cutting or reworking the fabric. The hook goes through the right side, picks up a loop from a yarn held at the back, and pulls a slip stitch up to the front. Work across the surface in a straight line, a curve, or a charted motif.
Hold the decoration yarn behind the fabric, against the wrong side. Make a slip knot and push the loop through the starting stitch gap from front to back so the loop sits on the hook at the front.
Insert the hook through the next stitch gap (or chain space). The hook goes through to the back of the fabric.
Wrap the hook around the back yarn and pull a loop through to the front. A slip stitch now sits on the surface.
Continue along the chosen path, one slip stitch per stitch gap. The line of slip stitches sits raised on the surface.
Common mistakes

attrs.heading: Slip stitch problems
attrs.intro: Five problems that come up across all four slip stitch uses.

items.symptom: The join round is visibly tighter than the body of the work
items.cause: Slip stitches pull naturally tighter than any other stitch.
items.fix: Use a hook one size larger for every slip stitch join. Swap back to the pattern hook for the next row.

items.symptom: The seam puckers or pulls the two pieces together
items.cause: Working too tight across matching stitches.
items.fix: Relax the tension on the join yarn. Each slip stitch should sit snugly against the edge but not gather it.

items.symptom: The surface crochet line wanders slightly off the intended path
items.cause: Uneven stitch gaps in the base fabric, or inserting into the stitch itself rather than the gap between stitches.
items.fix: Mark the path with removable stitch markers before starting. Insert consistently through chain spaces or between stitch columns, not through the stitch body.

items.symptom: Slip stitches across a travel run leave a raised line visible from the right side
items.cause: The travel stitches were worked with too much yarn tension.
items.fix: Loosen the travel row significantly. Each stitch should match the surrounding fabric height, not sit on top of it.

items.symptom: The round join shows a hole or gap
items.cause: The first chain of the turning chain was not worked snugly, or the hook missed the top of the turning chain on the join.
items.fix: At the start of the round, work the turning chain firmly. At the close, identify the top V of the chain carefully before inserting the hook.

content.text: What to try next

The natural next step from the slip stitch seam is the join-as-you-go technique, which uses slip stitches to attach a second motif to the first on the final round rather than seaming afterwards. For surface crochet, try drawing a simple zigzag across a swatch in a contrast colour first, then work a simple initial or border motif on a finished dishcloth.
